result: The multi-ancestry PRS was evaluated in 31,925 cases and 490,507 controls across multiple independent cohorts including MVP (21,078 cases, 284,177 controls), MADCaP (405 cases, 396 controls), and NCI-MD (383 cases, 395 controls), with representation from European (22,049 cases, 414,249 controls), African (8794 cases, 55,657 controls), and Hispanic (1082 cases, 20,601 controls) populations.
evaluation: Claims C13-C16 and C28-C33 provide consistent and detailed sample size information across multiple cohorts with appropriate citations. The large sample sizes and multi-cohort design strengthen the validation study. Sample sizes are internally consistent and well-documented.

result: The multi-ancestry PRS demonstrated strong associations with prostate cancer risk across all three populations, with odds ratios of 3.78 (European), 2.80 (African), and 3.22 (Hispanic) for men in the top PRS decile compared to average risk, and even stronger associations (ORs 7.32, 4.98, and 6.91 respectively) for men in the top percentile.
evaluation: Claims C17-C19, C38-C40, and C89 present consistent effect estimates with confidence intervals across populations. The large sample sizes (C13-C16) provide adequate statistical power. Figure 1 visually supports these associations showing clear dose-response relationships across PRS categories.

result: PRS associations were consistent across individual replication studies within each ancestry population, and adding the PRS to a base model of age and ancestry principal components improved the area under the curve by 0.136 on average across populations.
evaluation: Claim C41 is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing consistency across studies. Claim C42 provides a specific AUC improvement metric with reference to Appendix 1—table 1. The consistency across studies and meaningful AUC improvement support the robustness of the PRS.

result: The association between PRS and prostate cancer risk diminished with advancing age across all populations. In European ancestry men in the top PRS decile, ORs decreased from 7.11 (age ≤55) to 4.26 (age 55-60) to 2.79 (age >70), with similar patterns observed in African and Hispanic men.
evaluation: Claims C21-C24 and C45-C50 present age-stratified analyses with specific ORs and confidence intervals. Figure 2 visually demonstrates the attenuation of PRS effects with age. The consistent pattern across all three populations strengthens this finding. However, the biological mechanism for age-dependent effects is not explored.

result: Men in the top PRS decile reached 5% absolute prostate cancer risk approximately 8-12 years earlier than men in the average (40-60%) PRS category, with European ancestry men reaching this threshold 12 years earlier (age 57 vs. 69), African ancestry men 8 years earlier (age 55 vs. 63), and Hispanic men 11 years earlier (age 60 vs. 71).
evaluation: Claims C25 and C51-C54 present absolute risk calculations with specific ages referenced in Table 1 and Figure 3. The methodology (C37) describes use of SEER incidence and CDC mortality data. However, the absolute risk calculations depend on population-level incidence rates that may not reflect screening practices in the validation cohorts, introducing potential bias.

result: The PRS did not consistently discriminate between aggressive and nonaggressive prostate cancer. While some heterogeneity was observed (p-heterogeneity = 0.04-0.05), confidence intervals for aggressive vs. nonaggressive disease ORs overlapped in all populations.
evaluation: Claims C20 and C86-C88 present aggressiveness analyses with specific ORs and p-values for heterogeneity. The overlapping confidence intervals and marginal p-values (0.04-0.05) appropriately support the conclusion of no consistent discrimination. However, definitions of aggressive disease (C76-C77) may vary across cohorts, potentially affecting this analysis.

result: Compared to the mean PRS in European ancestry controls, African ancestry controls had a mean PRS associated with a relative risk of 2.19 (95% CI = 2.17-2.21), while Hispanic controls had a relative risk of 1.16 (95% CI = 1.15-1.18).
evaluation: Claims C43-C44 present population-level PRS differences with tight confidence intervals, consistent with prior findings (Conti et al., 2021). These differences help explain population-level disparities in prostate cancer incidence. The very narrow confidence intervals reflect the large control sample sizes.

result: This investigation provides the first evidence of PRS replication in Hispanic men. Lower PRS performance was observed in African versus European ancestry men, supporting the need to expand GWAS and fine-mapping efforts in African ancestry populations.
evaluation: Claim C55 correctly identifies novelty for Hispanic populations. Claims C56-C57 acknowledge lower performance in African ancestry men (OR 2.80 vs. 3.78 in Europeans, C18 vs. C17) and appropriately call for expanded research. The lower performance likely reflects the predominantly European ancestry composition of the original GWAS (C9: 75.8% European).

result: The stronger PRS associations observed in younger men suggest that genetic factors contribute more to prostate cancer risk at younger ages, and age should be considered when comparing PRS findings across studies and populations.
evaluation: Claims C58-C59 draw reasonable inferences from the age-stratified results (C21-C24, C45-C50). The interpretation is consistent with genetic architecture of complex diseases. However, alternative explanations (e.g., screening intensity differences by age, survival bias) are not fully explored.

result: Approximately 40% of men who will develop aggressive tumors are in the top 20% PRS category, while only ~7% are in the bottom 20% PRS category, suggesting that reduced screening among low PRS men may reduce overdiagnosis of prostate cancer.
evaluation: Claims C61-C62 present specific percentages with reference to Appendix 1—table 2, but the inference in C63 about reduced screening is speculative. The PRS does not discriminate aggressive vs. nonaggressive disease (C20), so low PRS men would have proportionally fewer cancers of both types. The claim requires prospective screening studies to validate.

result: The findings validate the multi-ancestry PRS as an effective prostate cancer risk stratification tool across populations, and clinical studies are warranted to determine whether the PRS could be used for risk-stratified screening and early detection.
evaluation: Claim C26 is supported by the strong associations demonstrated across populations (C17-C19, C38-C40). Claims C27 and C66 appropriately call for prospective clinical studies before implementation. The validation is robust, but clinical utility requires demonstration in screening settings with outcomes data.

result: The PRS was constructed by summing weighted allelic dosages of 269 prostate cancer risk variants using multi-ancestry conditional weights from a previous GWAS. Associations were evaluated using logistic regression with meta-analysis across studies, age-stratified analyses were performed in UK Biobank and MVP, and absolute risks were calculated using SEER incidence and CDC mortality data.
evaluation: Claims C34-C37 and C82-C85 describe appropriate methodology with proper citations. The PRS construction is reproducible (C84 provides PGS Catalog reference). Statistical methods (logistic regression, fixed-effects meta-analysis) are appropriate. However, no information on handling of missing variants across platforms or quality control thresholds for individual studies is provided.

result: The study utilized well-characterized cohorts with appropriate genotyping, quality control, and phenotype definitions. MVP included >800,000 participants genotyped on a custom Axiom array with imputation to 1000 Genomes Phase 3. Ancestry was assessed using HARE. Cases were identified from cancer registries with defined criteria for aggressive (T3/T4, N1, M1, or Gleason ≥8) and nonaggressive (T1/T2 and Gleason <7) disease.
evaluation: Claims C67-C81 provide detailed methodological information about cohorts, genotyping platforms, quality control, and phenotype definitions with appropriate citations. The methods are standard for genetic epidemiology studies. However, potential differences in case ascertainment across cohorts (e.g., MADCaP with late-stage cases, C78; NCI-MD with 87% nonaggressive cases, C80) could introduce heterogeneity.

result: Previous studies in men of European ancestry support that PRS-stratified screening could significantly reduce overdiagnosis of prostate cancer by 33-42%, with the largest reduction observed in men with lower genetic risk.
evaluation: Claims C64-C65 cite specific prior studies (Pashayan et al., 2015a; Callender et al., 2019; Pashayan et al., 2015b) with quantitative estimates. These are appropriately presented as prior work supporting the potential utility of PRS-stratified screening, though the current study does not directly test this hypothesis.

result: Background claims establish that prostate cancer is the second leading cause of cancer death in the US with significant health disparities, genetic factors play important roles in susceptibility and disparities, polygenic risk scores enable effective risk stratification for common cancers, and a previous multi-ancestry GWAS identified 269 risk variants that stratify prostate cancer risk.
evaluation: Claims C1-C12 and C60 provide appropriate background context with citations to support the rationale for the study. These are standard knowledge claims in the field and are properly attributed to prior work. The claims establish the scientific foundation for validating the multi-ancestry PRS.
